::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objective: Most children do not meet nutrition recommendations.
Primary schools are key settings for promoting healthy eating, but overlapping guidance can make it difficult to determine which food policies to adopt.
This study quantified which policy components are most effective, feasible, and tailorable to school and child needs, and identified mechanisms through which they influence behaviour.

Methods: A multistakeholder approach involved: 1) consultation with food policy experts; 2) scoping policies across England and Wales; 3) engagement sessions with primary school staff and children; and 4) triangulation of insights.

Fourteen policy components were identified and assessed for effectiveness (expert opinion; empirical evidence), feasibility (child endorsement; staff views; financial and resource demands), and tailoring potential.
Theoretical mechanisms were mapped to each component.
Results: Scores varied across components.
'Learning about food', 'role modelling', and 'eating with others' ranked highest, while 'growing food' and 'preparation or cooking food' were limited by cost and resource demands.
Five components had limited or no empirical evidence despite perceived feasibility.
Twelve components were rated as having moderate-tohigh potential for tailoring to school and child needs.
Six mechanisms were identified (exposure, food accessibility, motivation, social influences, and knowledge-and skills-based food literacy), each mapping onto multiple components.
This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring school food policy components, alongside the mechanisms.
Findings can support schools and policymakers in selecting and tailoring policies to diverse contexts.
Further research should test the proposed mechanisms and whether tailored approaches improve children's healthy eating.

It is well established that a nutritious and balanced diet, such as sufficient intake of fruit and vegetables, is critical for child health and significantly reduces the risk of noncommunicable diseases (1, 2).
text.formatted: It is well established that a nutritious and balanced diet, such as sufficient intake of fruit and vegetables, is critical for child health and significantly reduces the risk of noncommunicable diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: However, despite the current public health guidance available, many children globally do not meet nutrition recommendations (3).
text.formatted: However, despite the current public health guidance available, many children globally do not meet nutrition recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: For example, 91% of UK children do not consume the recommended five portions of fruit and vegetables each day (4).

Since dietary behaviours persist from childhood to adulthood (5) (6) (7), it is important to develop effective public health policies which encourage healthy eating behaviour as early as possible, to set children on a lifelong trajectory of better health.
text.formatted: Since dietary behaviours persist from childhood to adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>, it is important to develop effective public health policies which encourage healthy eating behaviour as early as possible, to set children on a lifelong trajectory of better health.

text.text: As highlighted in the WHO Health Promoting Schools framework (8), primary schools are a key setting for implementing evidence-based policies to improve children's healthy eating.
text.formatted: As highlighted in the WHO Health Promoting Schools framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>, primary schools are a key setting for implementing evidence-based policies to improve children's healthy eating.

text.text: A range of mandated and voluntary policies are used in schools, and evidence shows these can improve children's dietary behaviours, for example, increasing fruit and vegetable intake (9, 10).
text.formatted: A range of mandated and voluntary policies are used in schools, and evidence shows these can improve children's dietary behaviours, for example, increasing fruit and vegetable intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>.

text.text: In the UK, mandatory School Food Standards have been linked to healthier diets in young children (11).
text.formatted: In the UK, mandatory School Food Standards have been linked to healthier diets in young children <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, findings from a global modelling study suggest that introducing universal school meal provision by 2030 could substantially improve population health (e.g., preventing over one million cases of noncommunicable diseases) and reduce inequalities (e.g., reducing undernourishment by one quarter in food insecure populations) (12), underscoring the value of mandated approaches.
text.formatted: Moreover, findings from a global modelling study suggest that introducing universal school meal provision by 2030 could substantially improve population health (e.g., preventing over one million cases of noncommunicable diseases) and reduce inequalities (e.g., reducing undernourishment by one quarter in food insecure populations) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>, underscoring the value of mandated approaches.

text.text: Non-mandated policies, such as modelling, repeated exposure, and reward-based interventions (e.g., Food Dudes), also increase children's fruit and vegetable intake (13, 14).
text.formatted: Non-mandated policies, such as modelling, repeated exposure, and reward-based interventions (e.g., Food Dudes), also increase children's fruit and vegetable intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, healthy eating policies in primary schools can be effective, but there are several factors that influence policy decisions and effective implementation and affect their potential for improving children's healthy eating.

Whether or not a school food policy will ultimately improve children's eating depends not only on its evidence-based effectiveness but also how feasible it is to implement and how adaptable it is to the specific school context.

A school's resources, priorities, and local authority context all contribute to which policies are chosen and how policies are implemented and sustained, and effective implementation requires alignment with both school priorities and community characteristics (15).
text.formatted: A school's resources, priorities, and local authority context all contribute to which policies are chosen and how policies are implemented and sustained, and effective implementation requires alignment with both school priorities and community characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: The CONNECTS-Food system map highlights this complexity by identifying 27 school-related factors that independently and collectively influence children's diets (16), This underscores the value of providing schools and policymakers with clear, context-sensitive information to guide decisions about which policies are most likely to work in their setting and how they can be tailored to meet the distinct needs of the school environment.
text.formatted: The CONNECTS-Food system map highlights this complexity by identifying 27 school-related factors that independently and collectively influence children's diets <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>, This underscores the value of providing schools and policymakers with clear, context-sensitive information to guide decisions about which policies are most likely to work in their setting and how they can be tailored to meet the distinct needs of the school environment.

text.text: Beyond school characteristics, individual child differences influence the effectiveness and suitability of policies.
For example, strategies which involve sensory food exposure, which are effective for many, could be overwhelming or aversive for children with sensory sensitivity.
If strategies are not tailored to meet individual child needs, the potential for improving healthy eating is limited and could lead to unintended consequences (17).
text.formatted: If strategies are not tailored to meet individual child needs, the potential for improving healthy eating is limited and could lead to unintended consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, individuals with additional learning or feeding needs are more likely to need healthy eating strategies.
For example, autistic traits (18) and ADHD (19) in childhood have been associated with poorer diet quality.
text.formatted: For example, autistic traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> and ADHD <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref> in childhood have been associated with poorer diet quality.

text.text: Although some policies have been adapted for SEND settings (e.g., School Food Matters), and resources exist to support pupils with additional needs (e.g., Food a Fact of Life), there is currently no clear guidance for mainstream primary schools on which policies offer the most flexibility for meeting diverse child needs.
Qualitative research by Food Active (20) explored how to better support children with SEND during mealtimes in the Holiday Activities and Food (HAF) programme.
Although the UK School Food Standards offer a useful framework, they do not fully accommodate the diverse sensory, behavioural, and dietary needs of children with SEND.
This gap highlights the need for further work to understand whether school food policies are tailorable to the varied requirements of these children.
Insight into the mechanisms that underpin behaviour change can also assist with effective tailoring to context.
Many policies consist of multiple components spanning different areas of the school food environment.
For example, the Food Dudes intervention includes modelling, repeated exposure, and non-food rewards (13, 14).
text.formatted: For example, the Food Dudes intervention includes modelling, repeated exposure, and non-food rewards <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14)</ref>.

text.text: Although multi-component approaches may enhance impact, it is often unclear how individual components operate.
Understanding the critical mechanisms that drive behaviour change will assist in designing more targeted approaches by identifying which components should be preserved and which can be adapted (21).
text.formatted: Understanding the critical mechanisms that drive behaviour change will assist in designing more targeted approaches by identifying which components should be preserved and which can be adapted <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, identification of common underlying mechanisms may help schools maximise impact, as they can focus on a key behaviour-change process and implement relevant policies.

For example, providing food and delivering sensory education might both enhance healthy eating by increasing children's exposure to foods, which could be targeted by schools in ways that fit their context.
Evidence also suggests that policies operating through multiple mechanisms could be most effective, with greater potential for system-wide benefits (21).
text.formatted: Evidence also suggests that policies operating through multiple mechanisms could be most effective, with greater potential for system-wide benefits <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>.

text.text: This highlights the need to identify the behaviour-change mechanisms underpinning specific components of school food policies.
In summary, primary schools are a key setting for implementing effective interventions to improve children's healthy eating.

Schools already make numerous decisions about food policies, and the volume of existing guidance, which often overlaps, can create confusion about which policies to adopt, especially when policies are not mandated (15).
text.formatted: Schools already make numerous decisions about food policies, and the volume of existing guidance, which often overlaps, can create confusion about which policies to adopt, especially when policies are not mandated <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: To facilitate informed decision making about which policies are likely to be effective in context, research is needed on the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring of food policy components as well as the underlying mechanisms of action.

Rather than adding new policies to an already saturated area, we aimed to build on the existing landscape by adopting a multistakeholder approach aimed at improving understanding of what is likely to work, for whom, and why (22).
text.formatted: Rather than adding new policies to an already saturated area, we aimed to build on the existing landscape by adopting a multistakeholder approach aimed at improving understanding of what is likely to work, for whom, and why <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>.

text.text: Recent research highlights the value of using a multistakeholder approach.
For example, Spence et al. (23) found wide variation in perspectives among parents, school staff, and pupils on what works in the school food system and the challenges faced.
text.formatted: For example, Spence et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(23)</ref> found wide variation in perspectives among parents, school staff, and pupils on what works in the school food system and the challenges faced.

text.text: Including multiple perspectives also supports shared purpose and responsibility, which facilitates effective policy implementation (15).
text.formatted: Including multiple perspectives also supports shared purpose and responsibility, which facilitates effective policy implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we aimed to 1) identify key components of existing policies and evaluate them across a range of indicators to quantify the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring and 2) identify the potential mechanisms that might explain how each component operates to change behaviour.

A multistakeholder approach was taken: 1) consultation with food policy experts to provide insights and feedback about the project; 2) scoping of policies across England and Wales to identify effective policy components and the potential mechanisms by which policies may be working to improve healthy eating; 3) engagement sessions with stakeholders (school staff) and end-users (children) in primary schools in Birmingham, UK; and 4) triangulation of insights gained.
Throughout the project, we consulted a range of food policy experts.
The co-author SN is a food policy expert; therefore, we used her existing networks and contacts to identify relevant experts, who were invited to contribute via email.
In total, six food policy experts contributed to the project, including representatives from local authorities (n=2), academia (n=2), and a food policy consultancy (n=2).
These experts provided insights and feedback that supported the scoping of relevant policies and the design of, and recruitment for, engagement sessions (see sections 2.2 and 2.3 below).
Insights were captured through notes taken during informal online meetings.
Policy experts were also engaged through a webinar delivered to the UK Urban Food Forum.
Thirty individuals registered, representing more than 19 local authorities (n=21), the Welsh Health Boards (n=3), Welsh Government (n=2), the third sector (n=3), and academia (n=1).

In addition to presenting information about the project, we invited attendees to suggest policies that could be included in our scoping exercise and to discuss potential barriers and facilitators to implementation of policies.
Food-related policies to improve primary school children's healthy eating were scoped by KLE between February and July 2025.

'Policy' was defined as the legislation, laws, directives, guidelines, regulations, programmes, or voluntary initiatives that influence children's healthy eating, including public and organisational (e.g., school) policy.
Using a broad definition was important because schools may implement non-mandated strategies.
Healthy eating refers to nutritious food specifically (e.g., fruit, vegetables), or food that meets School Food Standards.
Policies were scoped via 1) engagement with experts in food-related policy, and 2) deskbased analysis of existing policies.
For the desk-based analysis, keywords for searches included "child", "healthy eating", "fruit," "vegetables", and "school food".
Policies were searched using Google, databases (e.g., gov.uk, FAOLEX), Microsoft Copilot, and academic literature (e.g., systematic reviews).

Findings from the content analysis are displayed in a comprehensive, open access resource (see https://airtable.com/appx23h5x1ViApEhv/shrzaJO1MdxK4nlrc/tbl6uJaO9X3VAJ1cG/viwlxwlTFgyCvPZkp).

text.text: Two focus groups were conducted with a total of six primary school staff.
Sessions were carried out in a local school and online (separately) to accommodate stakeholder needs.
Sessions lasted between 1-1.5 hours.
KLE facilitated the sessions, supported by a research assistant who took notes.
Staff worked in two primary schools in Birmingham, UK.
According to the Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index (IDACI) index, schools were in areas among the most deprived in England (top 10% and 30% most deprived).
Staff roles included head and deputy head teacher, teacher, teaching assistant, lunchtime supervisor, and business manager.
Based on NIHR guidance for involving people in research, each member of staff received £25 as payment for their time.
Sessions aimed to explore staff views about school food policies, to identify existing and effective characteristics, and to understand implemented feasibly.

Discussions explored: a) healthy eating policies used in local primary schools, b) barriers and facilitators of healthy eating policies in schools, c) factors influencing implementation and scalability of healthy eating policies, with questions structured around the COM-B model (24), and d) effective characteristics and future targets for policy development.
text.formatted: Discussions explored: a) healthy eating policies used in local primary schools, b) barriers and facilitators of healthy eating policies in schools, c) factors influencing implementation and scalability of healthy eating policies, with questions structured around the COM-B model <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(24)</ref>, and d) effective characteristics and future targets for policy development.

text.text: See supplementary material 1 for details of the focus group schedule.
Discussions and notes were summarised after each session.
Two workshops were conducted with children at two different primary schools in Birmingham, UK.
IDACI scores indicated that both these schools were in areas among the top 10% most deprived in England.
Sessions included 14 children in key stage 1 (aged 4-7 years) and 12 children in key stage 2 (aged 7-11 years).
Child engagement sessions explored whether children would enjoy trying different healthy eating strategies at school.

During the sessions, children were asked to stand at the 'thumbs up' station to show their endorsement of trying a specific healthy eating strategy, or to the 'thumbs down' station if they did not endorse it.
Some children also reported that they were 'unsure'.
A researcher then explored why children wanted to try, or not try, the healthy eating strategy at school.

At the end of the session, children completed a 'dotmocracy' task where they were asked to choose three strategies they would most like to try at school (see supplementary material 2, Figure A for an example).
text.formatted: At the end of the session, children completed a 'dotmocracy' task where they were asked to choose three strategies they would most like to try at school (see supplementary material 2, Figure <ref type="figure">A</ref> for an example).

text.text: Children were asked about the following ten healthy eating strategies which were identified from academic literature, policy scoping, and stakeholder sessions: learning about healthy food; eating with friends; trying a new food; having a reward for trying a new food; choosing what food to eat; going to breakfast club; having access to fruit and vegetables at breaktime; cooking healthy food; growing healthy food; or doing activities about food with parents at school.
Discussions and notes were summarised after each session.
The research team triangulated insights from multidisciplinary expertise gathered through consultations, engagement sessions, and policy scoping activities.
A one-day "research hackathon" held in July 2025 acted as a structured discussion and synthesis point.
Initial policy components and mechanisms were proposed by KLE and then collaboratively reviewed and refined by the research team.

Once the policy components and mechanisms were finalised, the team discussed and identified key indicators of policy components, which included effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring (see section 2.4.1. for details) and agreed on the approach for quantifying policy components.

text.text: The triangulation process was iterative and involved ongoing discussion and feedback within the research team throughout the project.

The in-depth discussions led to the selection of the following indicators: policy effectiveness (expert opinion and strength of the evidence base), feasibility (child endorsement, staff perceptions, and financial/resource demands), and potential for tailoring to meet school and child needs.
Effectiveness was assessed using expert opinion and the strength of the evidence base.

All policy experts were invited via email to complete a short online survey which assessed their perceptions of the effectiveness of, and strength of evidence for, each policy component in improving children's healthy eating; seven experts participated.

The strength of the evidence base was also assessed through literature searches conducted in August and September 2025 using online academic databases (e.g., Google Scholar) to identify rigorous reviews (e.g., systematic or scoping reviews) or meta-analyses for each component.
These searches focused on empirical studies examining individual policy components rather than evaluations of existing whole policies.

Feasibility was assessed using three indicators: child endorsement, drawn from engagement sessions with children; staff perceptions of feasibility, gathered from engagement sessions with school staff; financial and resource demands, based on findings from the policy scoping exercise (as documented in the https://airtable.com/appx23h5x1ViApEhv/shrzaJO1MdxK4nlrc/tbl6uJaO9X3VAJ1cG/viwlxwlTFgyCvPZkp).

text.text: The opportunity for tailoring was assessed through discussions among the research team, who reviewed how easily each component could be tailored to different school and child needs.

A heatmap table which includes each policy component was then developed to present the triangulation of insights, indicating the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring of each component.

For each indicator, all policy components were scored on a 3point scale with an associated colour code of dark green, light green, or yellow, except for 'empirical evidence' which was scored on a 4-point scale to capture the potential for evidence to show negative efficacy of policy components (i.e., unintended consequences; colour coded as red).
For example, the 'financial cost' of each policy component was scored as low, moderate, or high, and respectively colour coded as dark green (score=3), light green (score=2), or yellow (score=1).

The first author (KLE) led the analysis and had regular discussions with authors SN, JB, and SH to ensure methodological rigor, encourage critical engagement with the analysis, and reduce the risk of bias.
The initial table was developed by KLE.
Scoring decisions were noted and discussed with the research team to resolve discrepancies and achieve consensus.
The final heatmap table was reviewed and approved by the whole research team.

text.text: Using a multistakeholder approach, we quantified the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring of fourteen school food policy components and identified six mechanisms that explain how each component may operate to change behaviour.

The three policy components which were found to score highest across indicators of effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring were 'learning about food', 'role modelling', and 'eating with others'.
Nutrition education is part of England's national curriculum (29) meaning that children, staff, and policymakers are likely to be familiar with it.
text.formatted: Nutrition education is part of England's national curriculum <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(29)</ref> meaning that children, staff, and policymakers are likely to be familiar with it.

text.text: Indeed, 'learning about food' was also one of the most frequently identified components in existing policies.
Thus, greater familiarity with nutrition education could explain why 'learning about food' had the highest score when insights were triangulated.
This highlights the importance of mandating food policy into school practices and the curriculum.
'Role modelling' and 'eating with others' also scored highly on the overall ranking.
These individual components are likely to operate via social influences which have been consistently shown to influence eating behaviour (28).
text.formatted: These individual components are likely to operate via social influences which have been consistently shown to influence eating behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(28)</ref>.

text.text: School settings offer potential for a range of social experiences, such as with peers and staff, providing opportunity for use in a range of food contexts which could maximise improvements to healthy eating.
It is also possible that the effectiveness of policy components could be enhanced further if implemented in combination i.e. role modelling and eating with others.

Indeed, research has suggested that focusing on multiple areas of the school food environment may provide more sustainable impact of policies, especially if they target common underlying mechanisms (16, 21).
text.formatted: Indeed, research has suggested that focusing on multiple areas of the school food environment may provide more sustainable impact of policies, especially if they target common underlying mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>.

text.text: Other policy components were more variable across indicators.
For example, despite being perceived as feasible and tailorable, five policy components had no or low evidence to support them (i.e., no reviews or meta-analyses, or weak evidence).

Thus, our findings demonstrate several targets for future research to evaluate the effectiveness of specific components, including 'independent choices', 'training for staff', 'advertisements about food', 'school food culture', and 'parent engagement'.

In addition, some policy components achieved lower scores across several indicators, such as 'growing food' and 'preparation or cooking food', whereby the lower overall ranking was driven by high financial and resource costs and being more difficult to use.

This suggests that these components may be less likely to be implemented in schools, but importantly they are still likely to be effective if resources are available to support staff with implementation.

Promisingly, most policy components (n=12) were rated as having moderate to high opportunity for tailoring, suggesting that they may be suitable for a wide range of schools (e.g., those in areas of high deprivation) and children (e.g., supporting individuals with additional learning or feeding needs).
Aligning policies with school priorities and characteristics is important for effective implementation (15).
text.formatted: Aligning policies with school priorities and characteristics is important for effective implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: This is particularly important for supporting populations that are traditionally underserved, such as children living in deprived areas.
This issue is especially pronounced in Birmingham, where this study was conducted, with 62% of children living in households experiencing deprivation (30).
text.formatted: This issue is especially pronounced in Birmingham, where this study was conducted, with 62% of children living in households experiencing deprivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond local contexts, childhood poverty is also a major national and global challenge; for example, around one-third of children in UK classrooms are living in poverty (31).
text.formatted: Beyond local contexts, childhood poverty is also a major national and global challenge; for example, around one-third of children in UK classrooms are living in poverty <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the present findings offer an important step toward improving healthy eating for all children in schools by identifying potentially tailorable solutions that can be implemented across diverse settings, including schools in areas with high levels of deprivation.
Further work is now needed to codevelop practical guidance for policy tailoring.
We identified six mechanisms through which policy components may improve children's healthy eating.
Our conceptual model illustrates clusters of these mechanisms, with eight policies operating through multiple mechanistic pathways.
For example, both preparing or cooking food and growing food share the same underlying processes: increasing exposure and strengthening skills-and knowledge-based food literacy.

Evidence from Hawkes et al. (21) suggests that policies underpinned by several mechanisms are typically more effective, indicating that components with multiple pathways may be particularly valuable for school implementation.
text.formatted: Evidence from Hawkes et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref> suggests that policies underpinned by several mechanisms are typically more effective, indicating that components with multiple pathways may be particularly valuable for school implementation.

text.text: We also found clear cross-cutting mechanisms, with each mechanism mapping onto multiple policy components; for instance, exposure emerged as the primary pathway for eight distinct components.
A practical implication for schools is to focus on a specific mechanism (e.g., exposure) and implement some or all of the components linked to it.
Schools can also assess which mechanisms are already in place, identify gaps, and introduce additional mechanisms to strengthen existing approaches.
While our conceptual model highlights key primary mechanisms, additional pathways are likely to exist.
The model could be further refined and expanded to provide a robust framework for guiding policy selection, tailoring, and implementation in diverse school contexts.

The table provides a clear foundation for identifying relevant policies, comparing options, and making informed decisions about what to implement, and as such has the potential to function as a standalone toolkit or be integrated into existing school-food or whole-school health toolkits.
We have identified several gaps and priorities for future research.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the potential for tailoring policy components to the specific needs of individual schools and children.

text.text: Building on our results, future work should explore how policy components can be tailored within real-world school settings through consultation with diverse groups of children (e.g., those with additional learning or feeding needs) and key school staff (e.g., Special Educational Needs Coordinators [SENCo]).

Integrating these insights with the COM-B model (24) will help schools and policymakers to understand why policies may not be working for some individuals and highlight practical solutions to help policies be designed or tailored to meet varied child needs, or appropriate alternatives.

Applying a behavioural science lens, we developed a framework (Figure 1) that outlines the potential mechanistic pathways.

text.text: However, it is important to note that implementing and evaluating tailored policies can be challenging.

Whilst evaluation is recommended prior to large scale implementation, commonly using randomised-controlled trials and process evaluations (35), public health teams often lack the capacity to conduct such work.
text.formatted: Whilst evaluation is recommended prior to large scale implementation, commonly using randomised-controlled trials and process evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(35)</ref>, public health teams often lack the capacity to conduct such work.

text.text: In addition, evaluation measures may fail to capture broader psychological or social outcomes which could be indicative of later changes in dietary intakes.

For example, nutrition education may not immediately increase children's fruit and vegetable intake, but it could meaningfully improve food literacy as a precursor to long-term healthy eating behaviours.
There is a need for methodological approaches that support flexible implementation and evaluation across diverse contexts.
Stepped-wedge designs have been shown to be feasible for evaluating school-based interventions (36).
text.formatted: Stepped-wedge designs have been shown to be feasible for evaluating school-based interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(36)</ref>.

text.text: Realist approaches may also be valuable for understanding what works, for whom, in what circumstances, and how (37).
text.formatted: Realist approaches may also be valuable for understanding what works, for whom, in what circumstances, and how <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(37)</ref>.

text.text: These methodological advances, which use iterative and context-sensitive approaches, will help shift public health practice away from 'one size fits all' approaches and towards more effective, tailored guidance.

For example, schools may need to adjust policies during implementation and re-evaluate their impact on child health.

text.text: A key strength of this research was the inclusion of a wide range of perspectives including academics, policymakers, stakeholders, and end-users.
This coalition enabled the sharing of knowledge and views to develop a coordinated policy approach.
Engagement sessions were conducted in schools in Birmingham, UK, which is an area with high levels of deprivation (38).
text.formatted: Engagement sessions were conducted in schools in Birmingham, UK, which is an area with high levels of deprivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(38)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, IDACI scores indicated that schools included in stakeholder and child engagement sessions were in areas among the top 10% and 30% most deprived in England, meaning that perspectives from some under-represented were included, ensuring that findings are relevant for schools in areas with high levels of deprivation.

Although this research was grounded in Birmingham's policy context, which may limit generalisability to other local authorities due to differences in scale and resources, incorporating perspectives from UK-wide policymakers strengthens its potential for population-level impact through scalable interventions.
Stakeholder sessions included fewer primary school staff than intended due to challenges with recruitment.

To recruit stakeholders, we used local networks and contacts and made efforts to increase the accessibility of engagement sessions, such as hosting sessions in-person and online, offering travel expenses, and reimbursing stakeholders for their time.
Despite these efforts, recruitment was still challenging, often due to primary school staff having limited time and/or competing priorities.
Nonetheless, we were able to gain insights from a diverse range of staff and children.

Integrating insights from existing policies, empirical evidence, and multistakeholder perspectives, we evaluated fourteen school food policy components across indicators of effectiveness, feasibility, and potential for tailoring, and identified six mechanisms through which they may improve healthy eating.
Variation across indicators suggests that schools and policymakers should consider individual indicators when selecting components to ensure they meet school and child needs.
Our findings highlight the complexity of school food decision-making and provide practical resources to support more informed, context-sensitive policy choices.

Key next steps include testing the proposed mechanistic pathways, assessing what works in different contexts and for diverse learner needs, and strengthening collaboration between researchers, policymakers, and school communities.

Such collaboration is critical for implementing evidence-informed, feasible, and equitable policies that support children's healthy eating and create tools that enable rather than frustrate the complex school food system.
